newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-WMC H1 seen sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-WMC H1 seen sharply lower.

text.p: Falling world metal prices, a higher Australian dollar and cost overruns are expected to have battered the bottom line of base metals and gold group WMC Ltd in the six months to December 31, stock analysts said.
WMC, which reports its first-half results on Wednesday, has warned of weaker half year earnings.
Late last month, the company said global market sentiment for nickel, its key earner, had been pummelled by rising London Metals Exchange inventories.
Analysts' average forecast of WMC's first-half net profit before abnormals was A$111 million, down 40.4 percent from the A$186.2 million it reported for the same period a year ago.

"I think that the low nickel price will hurt substantially and I'm anticipating operating difficulties in the nickel operations and in the non-Alcoa of Australia alumina operations," said a Sydney-based analyst.
WMC owns 39.25 percent of alumina and aluminium producer Alcoa of Australia, which is controlled by the Aluminum Co of America.

First-half profit forecasts for WMC range from A$85 million to A$120 million, including gains of between A$40 million and AS50 million on WMC's hedging of the Australian dollar at US$0.75, analysts said.
The Australian dollar averaged US$0.79 during the half.

"We have (a forecast of) about A$115 million. If it's any lower than that ... I think the company's got a lot to answer for," said Richard Fish, resources analyst at National Australia Funds Management.

Analysts said WMC's nickel operations were unlikely to have made a large dent in costs during the half, despite managing director Hugh Morgan's pledge in November to slash 10 percent from nickel costs in 1996/97 (July/June).
"It is taking longer than they may have hoped," the Sydney analyst said.
WMC's total nickel production rose 10 percent in the first half to 118,790 tonnes but the average LME nickel price was 12.2 percent lower than for the first half of 1995/96.
Analysts also pointed to workforce restructuring costs at WMC's Kambalda nickel operation as another drag on profit.
Copper earnings are expected to fall on the back of a drop in first-half production to 44,669 tonnes and a slide in price.
Comex copper prices averaged 95.87 U.S. cents a pound for the six months to December 31.
"Obviously the lower copper price will hit Olympic Dam," one analyst said. Olympic Dam is the company's uranium, copper, gold and silver mine in South Australia.

WMC's gold unit is seen as another likely victim of weaker commodity prices. Analysts expect it to turn in a poor result, compounded by a slump in production from its Hill 50 operation in Western Australia. The mine is up for sale.
